_changelog: v1.0.0 (2026-10-07) first version. Season 1 finale case. Board cards use the catalog's three a1e09 concept ids (statelessness, context-window-as-the-only-memory, long-context-limits); strings reach back to context-windows (a1e05) and tokens (a1e03), and ahead to llm-apis (a2e01), trimming (a2e04), rag (a3e01), memory and summarizing (a4e03), prompt-caching (a6e03) and pii-in-prompts (a7e03). Honours the syllabus row: It Remembers Nothing, a hotel guest who forgets every morning. Every number traces to sims/a1e09-v1.0.0.js
title: It Remembers Nothing
setting: a hotel guest who forgets every morning

post.author: u/pigeonhole_severin
post.title: Every morning the guest in Room 12 remembers nothing, so my program reads him his notes at breakfast. At 6:52 today he walked out to meet a boat on a jetty that isn't there.

blocks.text: I'm a junior developer, and I work nights as the clerk at the Lindenmere, a lake hotel built in 1908. Mr Ostrander in Room 12 is 84. He has spent every summer here since 1961, and since an illness last year he keeps nothing overnight. He remembers 1961 perfectly. He doesn't remember yesterday.

When he arrived, his daughter Saskia wrote page 1 of a notebook: who he is, her number, and that he rows on the lake at seven every morning. Each night I add a page about his day. I built him a breakfast reader, a tablet that answers him in a calm voice, using a small model from a hosting service.

The model keeps nothing either, not even from one message to the next. So each morning my app sends it everything again: its instructions and his first question, 768 tokens, then the notebook. Its context window is 8,192 tokens, and I keep 1,024 back for the answer, which leaves 6,400 for pages.

On his tenth breakfast the notebook reached 6,750 tokens, and the tablet said nothing: the service refused the request as too long. So I changed my app, not the model, which never cuts anything itself: send page 1, then as many of the newest pages as fit. I'd read that models use the start and end of what they're given best.

06:31  request  breakfast 15   notebook: 15 pages, 10,300 tokens
                sent: page 1, pages 9-15   6,718 tokens
06:31  reader   Good morning, Mr Ostrander. Your boat will be at
                the jetty at seven, as always.

At 6:52 I saw him from the desk, walking out along the jetty in the fog. The storm on his seventh night took its last twenty metres. I ran. He was standing on the last plank above the black water, and he said the boy was late with the boat.

Page 8 is the night of the storm: the jetty is down, the boats are locked away, don't let him go out. It went in every morning since, apart from the silent one, until today. He's warm and asleep now, and Saskia is driving up. What happened, and what do I change before tomorrow's breakfast?

Top row, the notebook in three parts: page 1, Saskia's page, 1,000 tokens, sent; pages 2 to 8, 4,350 tokens, with page 8 saying the jetty is down, never sent today; pages 9 to 15, the newest, 4,950 tokens, sent. Bottom row: the instructions and his question, 768 tokens, go first into the request, 6,718 tokens in a window of 8,192. The reader answers at 06:31: your boat at seven, as always.

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Glad he's warm, and nothing on that jetty is haunted. Your guest and your model have something in common. The model is stateless: it keeps nothing from one request to the next. A chat only seems to remember because the app sends the conversation history, every earlier turn, meaning one message and its answer, back in with each new message, and the context window is the only room it has to hold it. You also half-remember a real finding that researchers called lost in the middle: in long inputs, models tended to use information at the start or end better than information in the middle. Read the paper's own setup before you build on it. Two questions. Pull up the requests for breakfasts 13, 14 and 15: which pages went into each, and where was page 8? And if you'd had the model boil the old pages down to a summary instead, what would that summary have kept?

replies.author: u/pigeonhole_severin
replies.text: Breakfast 13: page 1, then pages 7 to 13. Breakfast 14: page 1, then 8 to 14, with page 8 right behind Saskia's. Today: page 1, then 9 to 15. Each of those mornings the gap moved one page later, and today it reached page 8. And I tried the summary just now: I asked the model to boil pages 1 to 12 down to 300 tokens. It kept his name, Saskia's number, the crossword and rowing at seven every morning. It mentioned a storm. Not the jetty.

comments.author: u/boathouse_boy_mattias
comments.text: I was the boathouse boy at the Lindenmere from 1959 to 1964. Every morning at five to seven I rowed a skiff round to the end of the jetty for the gentleman in Room 12, and every morning he looked at his watch and said, you're late, boy. I never was. I'm 79 now. I heard the jetty went in the storm.

replies.author: u/pigeonhole_severin
replies.text: I read this to him at lunch. He asked whether Mattias still parts his hair on the wrong side.

comments.author: u/queue_lead_yusra
comments.text: We had a quieter version of this at work. Our support assistant was fine on short tickets, but on long threads it kept asking customers for their order number. The app dropped the oldest messages to fit the window, and the oldest message is where people say who they are and what went wrong. It took us five weeks to notice, because every answer was polite and fluent.

reply.prompt: Saskia arrives tonight, and the reader has a breakfast to do tomorrow. What should Severin change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Switch to a model with a 16,384-token window, so the whole notebook goes in every morning. Nothing gets skipped, and page 8 is always there for the reader to see.
options.part2: I moved the reader to a model with a 16,384-token window. Run on this morning's notebook, it sends all fifteen pages: 11,068 tokens, against 1,768 on his first breakfast, and every night adds another page to every morning after. For two mornings the reader told him the boats were put away. On the third it said seven o'clock again. Saskia caught him at the door. Page 8 sits in the exact middle of fifteen pages, and it was there to read. It just wasn't used.
options.senior: A bigger window buys time, not a plan. The history still grows every turn, so each request costs more than the last, and a fact in the middle of a long input is the kind models used least reliably in the lost-in-the-middle tests. Decide what must always reach the model.

options.text: Keep the newest pages that fit and drop the oldest first, the way most chat apps do. Page 8 is recent enough to make it in, and the latest pages matter most anyway.
options.verdict: Old isn't the same as unimportant
options.part2: I re-ran this morning's breakfast with the newest pages first: pages 7 to 15, 6,300 tokens of notebook, page 8 included and Saskia's page not. The reader said: good morning, sir, the boats are put away since the storm. He asked it where his daughter was. It didn't know he had one. Saskia read the answer over my shoulder and asked why it didn't know her name. And page 8 is now the second-oldest page it sends; every new night pushes it nearer the back.
options.senior: Dropping the oldest first assumes old means unimportant. Here the oldest page says who he is, and every page eventually becomes the oldest. Trimming by age loses whatever happens to be old, and nobody chooses what goes.

options.text: Each night, have the model fold every page older than the newest three into one short summary, so breakfast always fits and nothing is cut, only shortened.
options.verdict: Shortened by someone who wasn't told
options.part2: I set it up and ran it on this morning's notebook first: a 300-token summary of pages 1 to 12, then pages 13 to 15, 3,268 tokens, half of before. The summary was the one I'd already seen: his name, Saskia's number, the crossword, rowing at seven, a storm. No jetty. The reader told him his boat would be at seven. Saskia read the summary twice and asked who had decided what to leave out.
options.senior: A summary is written by a model, and it can keep the routine and lose the exception, as this one did. Summarizing saves tokens and keeps the gist, but whether one fact survives is left to chance. A fact that must not be lost needs a place of its own.

options.text: Write the facts that must never be missed on a short card sent first every morning, summarize older pages, keep the newest three, and check each request for the card.
options.part2: Saskia and I wrote the card together: 150 tokens. His name, her number, the jetty is down, the boats are locked away, no rowing. It goes first, every morning. Behind it come the 300-token summary and the newest three pages: run on this morning's notebook, 3,418 tokens, about half of before. A check runs every night on tomorrow's request and stops it if the card is missing. Saskia also took his medicines out of the pages the app sends, and the notebook is deleted the day he leaves. At 6:31 the reader told him the boats were put away for the winter. He asked if the boy had gone home. I said yes.
options.senior: Whatever a model must know shouldn't depend on where it falls in a long input, or on what a trim or a summary happens to keep. Pin the facts that change what it does, put them first, and check that every request carries them. Then shorten the rest to fit.

sim.title: Run the breakfast reader yourself
sim.lede: You're Severin at nine in the morning with the request log open. The notebook is Mr Ostrander's: page 1 is Saskia's, pages 2 to 15 are yours, each with its token count, and page 8 is the storm. Each breakfast the app sends the model its instructions and his question, 768 tokens, plus the pages a strategy picks, and keeps 1,024 tokens of the context window for the answer. Send everything is what the app did until breakfast 10: when the pages don't fit, the request is refused. Keep the newest drops the oldest pages first. Keep the first and last sends page 1, then the newest pages that fit. Summarize replaces every page older than the newest three with one 300-token summary, and a switch says whether the summary kept the jetty line. The card switch adds a short card of facts that must never be missed, 150 tokens, sent first. The reader is a toy: it answers from whether the jetty fact arrived, and whether it knows who he is. The position switch draws a recall curve inspired by the lost-in-the-middle finding: a teaching simplification with made-up heights, not the paper's numbers. Cost uses a teaching price of $2 per million input tokens.
sim.tryThis: Try this: you start on this morning, breakfast 15, window 8,192, keep the first and last. Page 1 and pages 9 to 15 go in, 6,718 tokens, page 8 is skipped, and the reader says the boat will be at seven. Slide back to breakfast 14: page 8 sits right behind page 1 and arrives. Back on 15, pick send everything: the request is refused, as on breakfast 10. Slide the window to 16,384: it fits, 11,068 tokens, and the total for fifteen breakfasts is 93,620 input tokens, about 0.19 dollars. Turn on the position curve: page 8 sits in the exact middle of fifteen pages and gets the lowest teaching value, 0.50. Set the window back to 8,192 and pick keep the newest: pages 7 to 15 arrive, page 8 among them, page 1 not, and the reader calls him sir. Pick summarize: 3,268 tokens, and the jetty is gone unless you switch on the summary keeping it. Last, turn on the card: 3,418 tokens, and the jetty fact arrives under every strategy, as long as the request isn't refused.

explain.oneLine: Nothing at the Lindenmere is haunted. The model behind the reader is stateless: each morning it knew only what Severin's app sent. When the notebook outgrew the window, the app sent page 1 and the newest pages, and this morning the gap reached page 8, the jetty. The reader answered from what it was given.

steps.title: The model is stateless: every request, it meets him for the first time.
steps.text: A language model keeps nothing between requests. It doesn't learn from a conversation while it talks, and it doesn't carry yesterday into today. Anthropic's documentation says it plainly: the Messages API is stateless, which means that you always send the full conversational history to the API. A chat seems to remember only because the app sends every earlier turn back in with each new message. The same docs describe each turn's input as all previous conversation history plus the current user message, with the answer becoming part of the input for the next turn. Engineers say the same of a web server that keeps nothing between requests: it is stateless, and whatever it needs arrives with the request or comes from storage. Severin's reader works this way. Each breakfast is a brand-new request, and the notebook is the only reason it knows Mr Ostrander at all.

steps.title: The context window is the only working memory, and the app fills it.
steps.text: Whatever the model is to use has to fit in its context window, case 5's limit, shared by the instructions, the history and the answer. Severin's window is 8,192 tokens: 768 for the instructions and the question, 1,024 kept back for the answer, 6,400 for pages. A conversation that keeps growing reaches that limit, and then the application has three choices: fail, trim or summarize. On breakfast 10 the notebook reached 6,750 tokens and the request failed. Anthropic's API does the same when the input alone exceeds the window: an error saying the prompt is too long. After that, Severin's app trimmed: page 1, then the newest pages that fit. The gap crept later each morning, and on breakfast 15 it covered pages 2 to 8, 4,350 tokens. The model didn't forget page 8. It was never shown it. The model itself doesn't trim; the software around it does, and often silently.

steps.title: Long context isn't perfect recall: lost in the middle.
steps.text: Nelson F. Liu and six colleagues tested how well models use long inputs. In one task, a question came with 10, 20 or 30 documents, passages from Wikipedia, exactly one of which held the answer, and they changed the order so that one sat first, last or anywhere between. In another, the model had to find the value for one key among 75, 140 or 300 key-value pairs. Performance was often highest when the relevant information was at the beginning or end of the input, and dropped when it was in the middle, even for models built for long inputs. With the answer in the middle, GPT-3.5-Turbo did worse than with no documents at all, which scored 56.1 percent. These were 2023 models, and newer ones may do better, but Anthropic's docs still warn that as token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade. Severin read the finding backwards. It is about where a fact sits among what was sent, so it argues for putting what matters at the start or end, not for dropping the middle. The sim's position curve is a teaching U shape inspired by the paper, with made-up heights.

steps.title: Every turn pays for the whole history again.
steps.text: Providers bill input tokens on every request, case 3's arithmetic, and a stateless model means the history is input every time. Had Severin's app sent everything in a window big enough, his first breakfast would have cost 1,768 input tokens and his fifteenth 11,068, and fifteen breakfasts would add up to 93,620: page 1 alone was paid for fifteen times. At the sim's teaching price of $2 per million input tokens that is about 19 cents, small for one guest and one request a day. A chat that resends its whole history with every message grows faster: when each turn adds about the same, the total climbs roughly with the square of the number of turns. Prompt caching exists to cut this. Anthropic's docs say it significantly reduces processing time and costs for repetitive tasks or prompts with consistent elements, and that cached prefixes still occupy the context window. A hit needs the beginning of the request to be identical, and by default the cache lasts 5 minutes, so it helps the turns of one conversation more than one breakfast a day. Season 6 covers caching.

steps.title: Memory is a feature you build: stored text, put back in.
steps.text: When a product says its assistant remembers you, it means the application stored something, such as notes, a summary or facts it pulled out of earlier chats, and puts the relevant part back into the prompt next time. Severin's notebook is exactly that, and so is a standing card: a few facts pinned to the top of every request. Choosing what to put back is the hard part. Season 3 builds retrieval, looking up only the stored text that matters for this question, and Season 4 builds memory for agents. Anthropic's API also offers compaction, in beta, which summarizes earlier parts of a conversation on the server. And what you store to remind a model is data about a person. Mr Ostrander's notebook holds his health, his family and his habits. Store only what the reader needs, with consent, and delete it when it's no longer needed.

diagram.aria: How a stateless model gets its memory, every turn. Top row: the conversation so far, stored by the app, here the notebook, goes to the app, which picks what to send by trimming, summarizing or pinning; what fits goes into the context window, the only memory, here 8,192 tokens. The model reads the window fresh and keeps nothing between requests. Its answer is saved back into the history for the next turn. Memory lives in the stored history, not in the model.

explain.caption: Read clockwise from the top left. The app keeps the conversation, here the notebook, and every turn it picks what to send. Only what fits in the context window reaches the model, which reads it fresh and keeps nothing afterwards. Its answer is saved into the history for the next turn. Memory lives in what the app stores, never in the model.

fix.title: The fix: pin what must reach the model, then shorten the rest on purpose
fix.text: Separate the facts that change what the model should do from the running history. Write them on a short standing card, review it with the people who know, here Saskia, and send it first in every request, where position works in its favour. Shorten the rest on purpose: a summary of older pages plus the newest few, or retrieval of the pages that matter, and count tokens before sending so a request never fails at breakfast. Then test it like any other code: a check on every request that the card is there, and a known-answer test, such as can I row this morning?, run against tomorrow's request before he wakes. Log what was left out each morning so a person can see the gap. Severin's card is 150 tokens; with the summary and the newest three pages, this morning's request would have been 3,418 tokens, about half of what it sent, with the jetty at the top. Keep the stored notebook small and private: only what the reader needs, deleted when he leaves.

limits: A card holds only what someone thought to write on it. The jetty went on after it nearly hurt him; the next danger is the one nobody has pinned yet. Review the card whenever a page says something changed, and keep the full notebook where a person reads it.

Position helps; it doesn't guarantee. In the lost-in-the-middle tests a fact at the start was used more often, not always, and a summary can drop anything. For a fact that could hurt someone, check the answer as well as the request.

Stored memory is personal data: this notebook holds his health and his family's number. Keep only what is needed, get consent from him or whoever acts for him, and delete it when he leaves. Standards readiness: GDPR data minimisation, the PDPA's retention limitation and ISO/IEC 27001's control on privacy and protection of PII (Annex A 5.34) all apply to it. Build them in now, not at audit time.

explain.seniorTake: A model remembers nothing. Your application remembers, and every turn it decides what the model gets to know. Treat that decision as design: pin what must never be missed near the start, shorten the rest on purpose, count tokens before sending, and test that critical facts arrive. And treat everything you store to remind it as personal data you are responsible for.

realWorld.title: Lost in the Middle, 2023
realWorld.text: Nelson F. Liu, Kevin Lin, John Hewitt, Ashwin Paranjape, Michele Bevilacqua, Fabio Petroni and Percy Liang analyzed the performance of language models on two tasks that require identifying relevant information in their input contexts. In multi-document question answering, the model got a question and k documents, for example passages from Wikipedia, where exactly one of the documents contains the answer; with 10, 20 and 30 documents, they adjust the order of the documents to change the position of the document that contains the answer. In key-value retrieval, the model had to find one value among 75, 140 or 300 key-value pairs. The models included GPT-3.5-Turbo and its 16K version, Claude-1.3 and its 100K version, MPT-30B-Instruct and LongChat-13B (16K). Their finding: performance is often highest when relevant information occurs at the beginning or end of the input context, and significantly degrades when models must access relevant information in the middle of long contexts, even for explicitly long-context models. With the answer in the middle, GPT-3.5-Turbo did worse than when predicting without any documents, the closed-book setting, 56.1 percent.

realWorld.title: More context, little gain
realWorld.text: The same paper, published in Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics in 2024, found that extended-context models are not necessarily better than their non-extended counterparts at using their input context, and that even base language models show the U-shaped curve. In a case study answering NaturalQuestions-Open questions from retrieved Wikipedia passages, using 50 documents instead of 20 retrieved documents only marginally improves performance: about 1.5 percent for GPT-3.5-Turbo and about 1 percent for Claude-1.3. The authors connect the U shape to the serial-position effect in psychology, where people recalling a list tend to best remember the first and last elements.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: the API keeps no conversation
realWorld.text: Anthropic's guide to the Messages API says it directly: the Messages API is stateless, which means that you always send the full conversational history to the API. Earlier turns are sent as alternating user and assistant messages, and they don't even have to come from the model: the guide notes you can use synthetic assistant messages. Whatever the app sends is, to the model, the whole conversation.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: how a conversation fills the window
realWorld.text: Anthropic's context windows page calls the window a working memory for the model and describes progressive token accumulation: as the conversation advances through turns, each user message and assistant response accumulates within the context window, and previous turns are preserved completely. Each turn's input contains all previous conversation history plus the current user message. If the input alone already exceeds the model's context window, the API returns a 400 error, prompt is too long, on every model; chat interfaces such as claude.ai can manage the window on a rolling first in, first out basis. The page warns that as token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade, which it calls context rot, and points long conversations to server-side compaction, in beta, which automatically summarizes earlier parts of the conversation on the server.

realWorld.title: Prompt caching
realWorld.text: Anthropic describes prompt caching as resuming from specific prefixes in your prompts, which significantly reduces processing time and costs for repetitive tasks or prompts with consistent elements, and lists long multi-turn conversations among its uses. Cache hits require 100% identical prompt segments up to the marked block, and by default, the cache has a 5-minute lifetime, refreshed each time it is used. The context windows page adds the catch: cached prompt prefixes still occupy the context window, so caching changes what you pay for those tokens, not whether they count.

realWorld.title: GDPR: only what is necessary
realWorld.text: The European Union's General Data Protection Regulation requires personal data to be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed, which it calls data minimisation. A memory feature that stores every conversation forever, just in case, starts on the wrong side of that line.

realWorld.title: Singapore's PDPA: stop keeping it
realWorld.text: Singapore's Personal Data Protection Commission explains the Retention Limitation Obligation in section 25 of the PDPA: an organisation must cease to retain documents containing personal data, or remove the means by which the data can be associated with particular individuals, as soon as it is reasonable to assume that the purpose is no longer served by keeping them and retention is no longer necessary for legal or business purposes. For Severin, that means the notebook goes when Mr Ostrander does.

asked: Does the model remember previous conversations?
How would you give a chatbot memory?
What happens when a conversation gets longer than the context window?
What is lost in the middle?
interview.answer: No. The model is stateless: it keeps nothing between requests, and it doesn't learn from a conversation while it talks. A chat seems to remember because the application sends the conversation history back with every message; with Anthropic's Messages API, for example, you always send the full history. To give a chatbot memory, I store text and put the relevant part back into the prompt: recent turns word for word, a summary of older ones, a few pinned facts such as the user's name and anything that changes what the model should do, and for a large store, retrieval of the notes that matter for this message. That stored memory is personal data, so I keep it minimal, ask for consent, and give users a way to see and delete it. When a conversation outgrows the context window, the application has to choose: fail with a clear error, trim, usually the oldest turns, or summarize older turns. I count tokens before sending, pin what must never be dropped, summarize the rest, and log what was left out, because a silent trim gives fluent answers that ignore what was cut. Lost in the middle is a 2023 finding by Liu and colleagues: when they moved one relevant document through 10, 20 or 30 documents, models used it best at the start or end and worst in the middle, even models built for long inputs. So I put the most important material first or last, keep inputs no longer than they need to be, and test with key facts placed in the middle of long inputs. Long histories also cost: every turn resends them as input tokens, so the total grows roughly with the square of the turns, and prompt caching can make a repeated beginning cheaper, though it still counts toward the window.

terms.def: Keeping nothing from one request to the next. Whatever a stateless model or server needs must arrive with the request or come from storage. Case 5 named it statelessness.
One message in a conversation and the answer to it. A chat is a run of turns.
Every earlier turn of a conversation, which the app stores and sends back to the model with each new message, because the model keeps none of it.
A 2023 finding by Liu and colleagues: in long inputs, models tended to use relevant information at the start or end better than information in the middle.
A company that runs language models, often open ones, on its own computers and sells access to them by the token. A kind of provider.
The fixed text an app sends with every request to tell the model its job and how to behave. Severin's take 768 tokens with the question.
Tokens of the context window an app keeps free for the model's reply, since the answer shares the window too. Severin keeps 1,024.
Here, a short text a model writes to stand in for older history, so a conversation fits. It keeps what the model chose to keep, and nothing else.
This case's name for a few facts pinned to every request, sent first, so they never depend on trimming or a summary. Severin's is 150 tokens.
To make sure a piece of text goes into every request, whatever else is trimmed.
As a product feature, text the application stores about a user or conversation and puts back into later prompts. The model itself remembers nothing.
Here, a program that uses a language model to take actions in steps, such as calling tools, over a long session. Season 4 covers agents.
A program, or the computer running it, that answers requests from other programs, such as a website answering a browser.
Anthropic's API for sending a model a list of messages, earlier turns included, and getting the next message back. Season 2 covers APIs like it.
An earlier turn written by the app rather than produced by the model, sent as if it were part of the conversation.
A provider feature that stores the processed beginning of a prompt, so an identical beginning sent again soon is cheaper and faster. Season 6 covers caching.
The beginning part of something. In prompt caching, the start of a request that must match exactly for the cache to be used.
A store of results kept for a short time so repeated work can be skipped.
Anthropic's server-side feature, in beta, that automatically summarizes earlier parts of a long conversation so it can continue past the window.
Done by the provider's computers, not by your own application.
A question whose right answer is agreed in advance, run against a system to check it. Here: can I row this morning? must get no.
A label and the value stored under it, like a word and its meaning. The paper's second task hid one pair among many and asked for its value.
A test where a model gets a question and several documents, only one of which holds the answer.
Answering from what a model learned in training alone, with no documents given. The paper's baseline for GPT-3.5-Turbo was 56.1 percent.
A version of a model made to take a longer input, such as GPT-3.5-Turbo's 16K version.
Short for context windows of about 16,000 and 100,000 tokens, in model names of 2023.
An OpenAI chat model from 2023, one of those tested in Lost in the Middle.
An Anthropic model from 2023, tested in Lost in the Middle with 8K and 100K windows.
An open instruction-tuned model from MosaicML with about 30 billion parameters and an 8K window, tested in Lost in the Middle.
An open chat model of about 13 billion parameters, extended to a 16K window, tested in Lost in the Middle.
A set of real search-engine questions with short answers found in Wikipedia, used to test question answering.
A finding in psychology: people asked to recall a list remember the first and last items best.
Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics, a research journal for language technology.
Anthropic's chat app for Claude.
Any information about an identifiable person, such as a name, a phone number, a health detail or a habit.
A person's informed agreement to their data being collected and used for a stated purpose.
The GDPR principle that personal data must be limited to what is necessary for the purpose.
The PDPA obligation to stop keeping personal data once its purpose is served and no legal or business need remains.
The European Union's General Data Protection Regulation, the EU's main law on personal data.
Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act 2012, overseen by the Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC).
The international standard for an information security management system. Companies are audited and certified against it.
Personally identifiable information: another name for personal data.
The list of security controls attached to ISO/IEC 27001. Control 5.34 covers privacy and protection of PII.
A formal check by an independent assessor that an organisation does what a law or standard requires.
The sim's made-up recall-by-position curve: a U shape inspired by the paper, not its measurements.
A wooden walkway built out over water, where boats tie up.
A small, light rowing boat.

atWork: Find one feature at work that talks to a model across turns: a support assistant, an internal chat, an agent. Read the code that builds each request: what history goes in, and what happens when it is too long? An error, a trim (from which end), a summary? Then send it the longest real thread you can find, with a key fact only in the first message, and see whether the answer uses it. If the feature stores per-user memory, list what it stores, who agreed to it, how long it is kept and how a user deletes it. Standards-readiness note: personal data in stored memory falls under data-protection duties such as Singapore's PDPA and the EU's GDPR, and, if your company is certified or heading that way, ISO/IEC 27001 controls on personal data. Building consent, retention and deletion in now costs far less than retrofitting them before an audit.

recall.prompt: Your company's support assistant handles long ticket threads. Customers complain that on long tickets it asks again for their order number and problem, though they gave both when they opened the ticket. Nothing errors. What's happening, and what do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The model keeps nothing between requests; the app resends the thread and, when it gets too long, drops the oldest messages, the customer's opening one with them
Pin the facts that matter, like the order number and the problem, so every request carries them near the start
Shorten older turns on purpose with a summary instead of silent dropping, and count tokens before sending
Test with long threads, check the key facts reach the model, and log what gets left out

recall.model: The model is stateless, so the app sends the thread again with every request. Once a thread outgrows the context window, the app is probably dropping the oldest messages to fit, and the oldest one is where the customer gave the order number and the problem. Nothing errors because a trimmed request still gets a fluent answer. I'd find the code that builds the request and confirm what it cuts. Then I'd pin the key facts, order number, product and the problem, onto a short block sent near the start of every request, summarize older turns on purpose instead of dropping them silently, and count tokens before sending. Finally I'd add a test with a long thread whose key facts sit only in the first message, check they reach the model, and log what gets left out each time.

recall.prompt: Why did the reader tell Mr Ostrander his boat would be at seven?
options: The model forgot page 8 overnight, the way he forgets each day
The app sent page 1 and the newest pages; page 8 wasn't among them
Page 8 was sent, but it sat in the middle, where the model skipped it
The service refused the request, so the reader guessed from habit
recall.why: The model keeps nothing overnight, so there was nothing to forget; it only knows what each request carries. This morning Severin's app sent page 1 and pages 9 to 15, 6,718 tokens, and skipped pages 2 to 8. Page 1 says he rows at seven, and nothing it saw said the jetty was down. The request wasn't refused: that was breakfast 10.

recall.prompt: A new teammate asks how a chat assistant can remember what they said ten messages ago when the model is stateless. Explain in plain words.

keyIdeas.idea: The model keeps nothing from one request to the next
The app sends the earlier messages back in with every new one
It all has to fit in the context window, so the app trims or summarizes long chats
Product memory is stored text the app puts back into the prompt

recall.model: The model itself keeps nothing between requests: every request starts fresh. The app stores the conversation, and every time you send a new message it sends the model the earlier messages and answers too, then your new one. That's how it knows what you said ten messages ago: it just read it again. All of that has to fit in the model's context window, so in a long chat the app has to trim older messages or summarize them, and whatever it leaves out, the model never sees. Features called memory work the same way: the app saves notes or summaries and puts them back into the prompt later.

recall.prompt: What did Liu and colleagues find in their lost-in-the-middle tests?
options: Models ignored every token past the first few thousand of the input
Models used a relevant passage best at the start or end, worst in the middle
Models built for long inputs used the middle as well as they used the ends
Models always used the newest passage best, however long the input was
recall.why: They moved the one relevant document through 10, 20 or 30 documents, and the key through 75, 140 or 300 key-value pairs. Performance was often highest at the beginning or end and dropped in the middle, even for explicitly long-context models. It's a measured tendency in 2023 models, not a law, and it is about position within what was sent.

recall.prompt: A chat app sends the whole conversation with every message, and each turn adds about the same number of tokens. How does the total of input tokens over a conversation grow?
options: It stays flat, because the provider only bills the newest message
It grows in step with the turns: twice the turns, twice the tokens
It grows faster and faster: twice the turns, about four times the tokens
It shrinks over time, because the model learns the conversation
recall.why: Each turn resends every turn so far, so the total is 1 + 2 + ... + n turns' worth, which grows roughly with the square of n. Severin's fifteen breakfasts with everything sent add up to 93,620 input tokens, while the fifteenth alone is 11,068. Prompt caching can make a repeated beginning cheaper, but those tokens still count toward the window.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. Mr Ostrander went home with Saskia in October, and the card went with him on paper. My day job has pulled me onto a hotel group's guest assistant. My teammate Bertil wants it to remember guests between stays, so he plans to keep every conversation every guest has ever had and send each guest's whole history with every message. Some of those chats mention health, children, a funeral someone came to town for. Nobody has been asked. He says storage is cheap and the windows are huge now.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What would you tell Bertil, and what would you build instead?

keyIdeas.idea: The model remembers nothing; memory is stored text the app chooses to put back, so choose: pinned facts, a summary, or retrieval of the relevant notes
Sending every past conversation costs input tokens on every message, can still overflow the window, and buries what matters in the middle
Those chats are personal data, some about health: get consent, keep the minimum, set a retention period and let guests see and delete it
Test that the facts that matter actually reach the model

coldCase.model: The model won't remember anything; the app does, by storing text and choosing what to put back into each request. Sending every past conversation is the wrong choice. It costs input tokens on every message, growing with every stay; some histories will still overflow the window; and a guest's one important preference ends up buried in the middle of a long input, where models use information least reliably. I'd build memory on purpose: a short profile of pinned facts the guest has confirmed, such as dietary needs, room preferences and accessibility, a summary of past stays, and retrieval of only the notes relevant to the current message. Those chats are personal data, some of it about health, so the guest should opt in, we keep the minimum, set a retention period, and give guests a way to see and delete what we hold. That lines up with data minimisation under the GDPR, retention limitation under the PDPA, and ISO/IEC 27001 controls if we're certified. Then I'd test it: put a key fact in an old stay and check that it reaches the model when it should.

sources.title: Liu, Lin, Hewitt, Paranjape, Bevilacqua, Petroni and Liang, Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts, arXiv 2307.03172 (v3, November 2023): two tasks, multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval; k documents, exactly one containing the answer, 10, 20 and 30 documents, reordered to move the relevant one; 75, 140 and 300 key-value pairs; models GPT-3.5-Turbo (4K and 16K), Claude-1.3 (8K and 100K), MPT-30B-Instruct (8K), LongChat-13B (16K); performance often highest when relevant information occurs at the beginning or end and significantly degrades in the middle, even for explicitly long-context models; GPT-3.5-Turbo with the answer in the middle below its closed-book performance, 56.1%

Liu and colleagues, Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts, Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics, volume 12, pages 157 to 173, 2024 (DOI 10.1162/tacl_a_00638): extended-context models are not necessarily better than their non-extended counterparts at using their input context; even base language models show a U-shaped curve; using 50 instead of 20 retrieved documents only marginally improves performance, about 1.5% for GPT-3.5-Turbo and about 1% for Claude-1.3; the serial-position effect

Anthropic, Using the Messages API (Claude Platform docs), Multiple conversational turns: the Messages API is stateless, which means that you always send the full conversational history to the API; earlier turns can be synthetic assistant messages

Anthropic, Context windows (Claude Platform docs): a working memory for the model; progressive token accumulation, each user message and assistant response accumulates and previous turns are preserved completely; input phase contains all previous conversation history plus the current user message; input alone over the window returns a 400 invalid_request_error, prompt is too long, on every model; chat interfaces such as claude.ai can manage the window first in, first out; context rot; cached prompt prefixes still occupy the context window; server-side compaction in beta summarizes earlier parts of the conversation

Anthropic, Prompt caching (Claude Platform docs): resuming from specific prefixes in your prompts significantly reduces processing time and costs for repetitive tasks or prompts with consistent elements; useful for long multi-turn conversations; cache hits require 100% identical prompt segments; by default the cache has a 5-minute lifetime, refreshed for no additional cost each time it is used

Regulation (EU) 2016/679, the General Data Protection Regulation, Article 5(1)(c): personal data shall be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed (data minimisation)

Personal Data Protection Commission Singapore, Advisory Guidelines on Key Concepts in the PDPA, Chapter 18, The Retention Limitation Obligation (section 25 of the PDPA): cease to retain documents containing personal data, or remove the means by which it can be associated with particular individuals, once the purpose is no longer served and retention is no longer necessary for legal or business purposes; not kept just in case

ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Information security, cybersecurity and privacy protection, Information security management systems, Requirements: requirements for establishing, implementing, maintaining and continually improving an information security management system; Annex A includes control 5.34, privacy and protection of PII
